You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.

# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Change the image into pencil drawing
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Are the scene's principal shapes and meaningful internal boundaries represented with convincing pencil-like contour linework?
node.criteria: Pass if pencil-like contour strokes broadly describe the principal forms and meaningful internal boundaries across the scene. Evidence may include fine irregular graphite-like lines, sketch-like stroke articulation or variable line weight. Contours may follow the source image's boundaries: preserving their geometry does not disqualify a pencil-drawn rendering. Every boundary need not be outlined, and some soft edges may remain. Fail if the principal boundaries still appear photographic or merely sharpened, without broadly convincing drawn linework. Reduced saturation, uniform grain and stronger photographic edges alone do not satisfy this condition. Assess contour appearance independently of interior shading. Use unknown only when visual evidence is insufficient to establish the contour style.
node.binding: Compare the supplied SOURCE and EDITED images against the requested pencil-drawing transformation. Inspect the plate rim, potato-slice perimeters and internal marks, carrot boundaries, fork tines, and glass and pitcher outlines. Compare the character and extent of the edited boundary strokes with the corresponding source edges, distinguishing pencil-like lines from photographic edge contrast or sharpening halos. Base the decision on these visible contours, not on color reduction, overall grain, retained source geometry or whether interior shading is complete. The target is pencil-drawn representation of the image's visual content; the reference is the supplied image and the requested pencil-drawing transformation.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image is desaturated and grainy, but the plate rim, food perimeters, fork tines, and glass and pitcher outlines mostly retain soft photographic edges. They do not show broadly convincing pencil-like contour strokes or sketch articulation; the grain and edge contrast alone are insufficient.

d1_shading: The binding is truncated/underspecified (“(...)”), which can leave the decision without a clear comparison target. Restore an explicit, self-contained binding to the requested pencil-drawing transformation and the supplied source/edit pair. The trace is valid and has no transport or dependency failure, so focus on visual criterion calibration: the edit clearly progresses beyond the source through desaturation, softened tones, and grain, but the trace identifies retained smooth photographic gradients and reflections and little directional graphite shading across major surfaces. Do not treat grain or outlines alone as completion, but distinguish partial stylistic progress from no progress; assess the overall transformation rather than making one imperfect surface decisive. Keep the shading criterion explicit and evaluate evidence across the scene, using unknown only if the images do not permit a reliable judgment. The high-confidence “no” despite visible progress suggests the node’s decision boundary or partial-progress routing needs investigation; confidence itself is not evidence that the requested edit is absent.
